A new documentary on Apple TV, "All of Us," tells the story of a public elementary school that educates students with diverse needs in a unique way.

Both iPhone and iPad are key tools that make this model, hailed as a successful example of inclusive education, possible...

Students with special needs are often separated from mainstream students for instruction because of their disabilities. The traditional belief is that putting everyone in the same classroom would be disruptive for the majority of students.

Ruby Bridges Elementary takes a very different view. In fact, inclusive teaching does not cause disruption; rather, it benefits all students academically and socially. The success of this model is so significant that the school's principal and a kindergarten teacher were named Principal of the Year and Teacher of the Year in 2025, respectively.

A 70-minute documentary streaming on Apple TV tells the story of "a school that breaks the mold."

At Ruby Bridges, all students learn together in general education classrooms. Every child does math together, reads together, and sings together in music class. Teachers and specialists work closely together in the classroom, and the results speak for themselves. So how exactly do they do it? Ruby Bridges Elementary is a public school. Apart from the school's own resources, there is no extra funding or staff, and there is no magic solution. It is simply a group of educators who decided to stop separating children and chose to believe in the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mold—a school that is unique but should not have to be unique.

iPad and iPhone play a key role

Some students have severe communication difficulties, and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) apps running on iPad and iPhone have dramatically enhanced their ability to interact with teachers and other classmates.

An important finding is that AAC apps are not only useful for students with communication difficulties, but are equally effective for all students. Founding principal Cathi Davis told me:

"All students—whether they are highly literate or just beginning to develop communication or language—show an extremely high level of engagement when they can use AAC tools to generate, expand, or express their ideas. With this tool that supports communication at any time, we can overcome challenges such as writing skills, writing stamina, and the anxiety of speaking out loud, while also overcoming various obstacles that arise in the classroom or in life... This truly embodies the essence of what we call 'universal design.' Compared to almost any other language, communication, or vocabulary tool in the classroom, it is truly a tool for everyone."

As the documentary reveals, this teaching model works for all students—not just those with special needs—and this is indisputable. The documentary's dedicated website also offers a comprehensive set of video resources for other schools interested in following Ruby Bridges' example.
